title: Can a Startup Sponsor an H-1B? Requirements, Cost, and Timeline
body_markdown:
Yes. A startup can sponsor an H-1B — at pre-seed, seed, Series A, or any later stage. There is no minimum revenue threshold, no minimum headcount, no requirement to be a "large employer." Any U.S. entity with a valid FEIN can theoretically file an H-1B petition on behalf of a qualifying beneficiary.


But USCIS scrutinizes startup H-1B petitions more carefully than it does petitions from large established companies. The most common reason a startup H-1B gets denied or hit with a Request for Evidence isn't ineligibility — it's under-preparation on three specific dimensions that adjudicators look at closely: ability to pay, the specialty-occupation nature of the role, and the bona fide employer-employee relationship.


This post walks through eligibility, cost, timeline, and the six startup-specific pitfalls that trip up first-time sponsoring companies.


## The Short Answer — Yes, but With Conditions


A startup can sponsor an H-1B when three things are true:


1. The company can demonstrate ability to pay the offered prevailing wage for the duration of the petition (typically 3 years)
2. The role qualifies as a specialty occupation under the[H-1B Modernization Rule's "directly related" degree standard per Buchalter](https://www.buchalter.com/insights/what-the-h-1b-modernization-rule-means-for-employers-and-employees/)
3. The employer-employee relationship is documented and — for founder-owned petitioners — meets the new owner-beneficiary framework created by the[2025 H-1B Modernization Rule](https://www.uscis.gov/newsroom/alerts/h-1b-final-rule-h-2-final-rule-and-revised-form-i-129-effective-jan-17-2025)


Get these three right and the H-1B is very achievable for a startup. Get them wrong and you face RFEs, denial, or wasted lottery selection.


### What the Startup Needs — The Employer Eligibility Checklist


Six requirements the sponsoring startup itself must satisfy.


#### 1. Valid U.S. Employer


The company must be a U.S.-incorporated entity with a valid Federal Employer Identification Number and a physical U.S. business address. Virtual offices and shared co-working spaces are scrutinized for startups — USCIS wants evidence of a real business operating at a real location.


#### 2. Sufficient Runway or Revenue to Pay the Offered Wage


USCIS may issue an RFE requesting documentation that the startup can pay the prevailing wage for the full validity period. Acceptable evidence includes bank statements, funding announcements, term sheets, revenue statements, and audited financials. A recently closed seed or Series A round with proof of funds in the bank typically satisfies this.


#### 3. A Bona Fide Specialty Occupation Role


The role must require at least a U.S. bachelor's degree (or foreign equivalent) in a specific field directly related to the duties. Per the[2025 H-1B Modernization Rule as summarized by Buchalter](https://www.buchalter.com/insights/what-the-h-1b-modernization-rule-means-for-employers-and-employees/) , USCIS defines "directly related" as having "a logical connection" between the degree and the role, and a job that accepts a degree in "any field" no longer qualifies. This standard has real teeth at startups where roles are often generalist.


#### 4. DOL-Certified Labor Condition Application (LCA)


Before filing the H-1B petition, the employer must file an LCA with the Department of Labor stating the wage, worksite, and role. The LCA is filed on Form ETA 9035 or 9035E per[20 CFR §655.731](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/20/655.731) .


#### 5. Public Access File Within One Business Day


Every LCA requires a Public Access File. Per[RN Law Group's PAF guidance](https://www.rnlawgroup.com/what-is-a-public-access-file-paf-employer-requirements-and-how-to-respond-to-requests/) , the PAF must include the certified LCA, wage rate documentation, prevailing wage source, actual wage system explanation, proof of notice posting, and a summary of benefits — created within one business day of LCA submission and retained for at least one year past the LCA validity period.


#### 6. Prevailing Wage Compliance


The employer must pay at least the greater of the actual wage paid to similar employees or the DOL prevailing wage for the role and geographic area of employment. Per[8 U.S.C. §1182(n)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/20/655.731) , this is a per-hour, per-worksite obligation with no exceptions for startups.


### What the Beneficiary Needs — The Candidate Eligibility Checklist


Four requirements the H-1B candidate must meet.


#### 1. A U.S. Bachelor's Degree or Foreign Equivalent Directly Related to the Specialty Role


A U.S. master's, credentialing equivalency, or specialized experience can substitute in specific circumstances but requires documentation. The degree field must be directly related to the role — not tangentially related.


#### 2. The Role Requires the Degree


It's not enough for the beneficiary to have a degree — the role must genuinely require it. "Preferred" doesn't cut it.


#### 3. Wage Compliance


The offered wage must meet or exceed the DOL prevailing wage for the role and worksite.


#### 4. Cap Eligibility


For new H-1Bs, the beneficiary must be selected in the March lottery. Beneficiaries who already hold cap-exempt H-1B status (e.g., from a university appointment) can be sponsored by a for-profit startup concurrently without entering the lottery — a workaround covered in the H-1B Cap-Subject vs. Cap-Exempt companion post.


### The Cost Breakdown — 2026 Fully-Loaded


#### Government Fees (Paid by Employer, Cannot Be Passed to Worker)


Per the[USCIS I-129 fee schedule](https://www.uscis.gov/forms/all-forms/h-and-l-filing-fees-for-form-i-129-petition-for-a-nonimmigrant-worker) :


- I-129 base filing fee: $780 (paper) / $730 (online)
- ACWIA training fee: $750 for employers with fewer than 25 FTEs, $1,500 for 25+ FTEs
- Fraud prevention & detection fee: $500 (initial petitions and change-of-employer)
- Asylum Program Fee: $300 for small employers (25 or fewer FTEs), $600 for larger employers, exempt for nonprofits
- H-1B registration fee: $215 per beneficiary (cap-subject only)


#### Optional but Common


- Premium processing:[$2,965 as of March 1, 2026 per VisaHQ](https://www.visahq.com/news/2026-03-01/us/uscis-premium-processing-fees-jump-as-new-rule-takes-effect/) — reduces adjudication time to 15 business days


#### Legal Fees (Fixed-Fee Firm)


- Startup-focused AI-native firm: $2,500–$5,000 per petition
- Traditional BigLaw: $4,000–$8,000+ per petition


#### Startup All-In Totals (Cap-Subject H-1B, Small Employer With Fewer Than 25 FTEs)


- Without premium processing: ~$5,000–$8,000
- With premium processing: ~$8,000–$11,000


For a role commanding a $150K+ salary, the H-1B is roughly 3–7% of first-year compensation — a rounding error against the cost of losing the candidate or paying a recruiter to source a replacement.


### The Timeline for a Cap-Subject Startup H-1B


For any startup planning to sponsor a new H-1B in the FY 2028 cycle:


- Q4 2026 (Oct–Dec): Identify candidate, run pre-lottery eligibility check, confirm role and prevailing wage
- January–February 2027: Prepare registration materials, verify beneficiary documentation
- March 2027: USCIS registration window (~2 weeks, historically first half of March based on the[FY 2027 window of March 4–19, 2026 per Mintz](https://www.mintz.com/insights-center/viewpoints/2806/2026-02-02-uscis-announces-h-1b-cap-registration-period-march-2026) )
- Late March 2027: Selection notification — historical selection rate around 35.3% based on FY 2026 USCIS data
- April–June 2027: File I-129 petition (90-day window from selection)
- Adjudication: 15 business days with premium processing, or 4–8 months standard
- October 1, 2027: Earliest work start date


For cap-exempt startups — rare, but possible when the startup is a nonprofit research organization, a university-affiliated entity, or a governmental research organization — the timeline compresses dramatically. Cap-exempt H-1B petitions can be filed year-round, and the beneficiary can start work as soon as USCIS approves. See the H-1B Cap-Subject vs. Cap-Exempt post for the full breakdown.


### The 6 Common Startup-Specific Pitfalls


Six mistakes account for the vast majority of startup H-1B denials and RFEs. Design around all of them from the start.


#### 1. Insufficient Runway to Demonstrate Ability to Pay


USCIS routinely issues RFEs asking the startup to prove it can pay the offered prevailing wage for the full H-1B validity period. Have ready:


- Recent bank statements showing runway
- Fundraise announcements or term sheets
- Revenue statements or audited financials (if applicable)
- Cash flow projections showing the wage is sustainable


Pre-seed or bootstrapped startups often struggle here. If runway is thin, either strengthen the documentation upfront or delay the filing.


#### 2. Vague or Non-Specialty Roles


"Software Engineer" at a 5-person startup where the beneficiary is doing full-stack development, product design, DevOps, and customer support triggers scrutiny. USCIS wants to see:


- A specific specialty-occupation job title
- A detailed role description showing degree-required complexity
- A direct connection between the beneficiary's degree field and the role's core duties
- Evidence the role would not be filled by someone without the required degree


Per the[2025 Modernization Rule per Immigration Start Guide](https://immigrationstartguide.com/blog/h1b-modernization-rule) , requiring a degree in "business, economics, engineering, or a related field" without explanation no longer establishes specialty occupation on its own — USCIS wants a logical connection between the specific degree and the specific role.


Startups should draft job descriptions with H-1B eligibility in mind from Day 1.


#### 3. Founder as Beneficiary Without Owner-Beneficiary Planning


Before January 17, 2025, a founder who owned more than 50% of the sponsoring company was effectively locked out of the H-1B because USCIS couldn't establish an employer-employee relationship. The[H-1B Modernization Rule per Gilt Law](https://www.giltlaw.com/2025/02/h-1b-modernization-rule-entrepreneurs-your-h-1b-dreams-can-be-a-reality/) removed the common-law employer-employee test and created a real pathway for owner-beneficiaries.


Key mechanics of the owner-beneficiary H-1B:


- Founders owning more than 50% or holding majority voting rights can be sponsored
- Initial approval is limited to 18 months (vs. 3 years for standard H-1B)
- Extension for another 18 months, then in 3-year increments
- The founder must be performing a bona fide specialty occupation role
- Standard specialty-occupation and prevailing-wage requirements still apply
- Petition still enters the cap-subject lottery


Many founders are better served by the O-1A, which has no lottery, longer initial validity, and no wage constraints. Walk through the decision in the H-1B vs. O-1A for Founders companion post before defaulting to H-1B.


#### 4. Virtual Office as the Worksite


USCIS scrutinizes virtual or co-working addresses at startups. Adjudicators want evidence of a real physical business — signage, a lease, employees on-site, equipment. A pure WeWork address with no other indicators of physical operations is a red flag.


##### If Your Startup Is Fully Remote


- Document the beneficiary's actual home worksite
- Ensure the LCA covers the actual worksite location (post-Matter of Simeio Solutions, worksite outside the LCA-covered area requires an amended petition)
- Prepare to explain the remote-work structure clearly in the petition


##### If the Startup Uses a Co-Working Space


- Have a real desk assignment, not just a mailing address
- Document the physical presence of the company
- Consider whether the beneficiary's actual worksite (home office, coffee shop, client site) should be the LCA-listed worksite instead


#### 5. Missing or Incomplete Public Access File


The LCA Public Access File is the most-audited compliance artifact in H-1B sponsorship, and it's the one first-time-sponsoring startups miss most often. Every LCA requires a PAF created within one business day of filing and retained for at least one year past the LCA validity period.


Per[RN Law Group](https://www.rnlawgroup.com/what-is-a-public-access-file-paf-employer-requirements-and-how-to-respond-to-requests/) , the PAF must contain:


- Certified LCA (ETA Form 9035 or 9035E)
- Wage rate documentation and how the wage was determined
- Prevailing wage source and actual wage system explanation
- Proof of notice posting
- Summary of benefits available to U.S. and H-1B workers in the same classification


Build the PAF checklist into your workflow. Every LCA triggers a PAF. No exceptions.


#### 6. Missing the March Registration Window


For cap-subject candidates, missing the March registration window means waiting a full year to file. The[FY 2027 registration window ran March 4–19, 2026 per Mintz](https://www.mintz.com/insights-center/viewpoints/2806/2026-02-02-uscis-announces-h-1b-cap-registration-period-march-2026) . The FY 2028 window will run in March 2027.


First-time sponsors should mark the following on the calendar in Q4:


- Late January / early February: Confirm candidate list and prepare registration payment
- Late February: Verify all beneficiary information and USCIS account access
- Early March: Register at the opening of the window
- Late March: Watch for selection notification
- April–June: File the I-129 petition within the 90-day window


Missing the window is one of the most preventable mistakes in H-1B sponsorship and one of the most expensive.


### When the H-1B Isn't the Right Visa


The H-1B isn't the only option, and it isn't always the best one. Common alternatives for startup situations:


- Founder with press, funding, or awards: Consider the O-1A — no lottery, faster, no prevailing wage. See the H-1B vs. O-1A for Founders companion post for the full decision framework.
- Australian nationals: Consider the E-3 — Australia-specific, no lottery, faster, two-year renewable status.
- Canadian or Mexican nationals in listed professional occupations: Consider the TN — fast, cheap, no lottery.
- F-1 student on OPT: Post-completion OPT provides 12 months of work authorization, and STEM OPT extends it by 24 months. This can bridge the beneficiary to a later H-1B or O-1A filing without needing immediate sponsorship.
- Candidate already at a cap-exempt employer: Consider concurrent H-1B employment. A candidate holding a cap-exempt H-1B — for example, a research role at a university — can be sponsored by a for-profit startup concurrently without entering the lottery. Full breakdown in the H-1B Cap-Subject vs. Cap-Exempt post.
- Candidate with intracompany transfer history: If the beneficiary spent at least one continuous year at a qualifying foreign affiliate in the past three years, the L-1 (executive/manager or specialized knowledge) may be a faster path.
- Candidate qualifying for extraordinary ability: For senior technical hires with strong recognition profiles, the O-1A is often faster and cleaner than H-1B — even outside the founder context.


### Should the Startup Sponsor a Green Card Too?


Most sponsored H-1B employees will need green card sponsorship within a few years to stay long-term. Filing PERM early — at 12 to 18 months of tenure — is one of the highest-ROI retention decisions a startup can make, especially given[PERM currently takes about 402 days on average per PermQueue](https://permqueue.com/blog/how-long-does-perm-take-2026) and priority dates for backlogged countries can add years on top of that.


For high-impact employees, evaluating EB-1A or EB-2 NIW self-petitions in parallel with employer-sponsored PERM is standard practice at competitive companies — full retention framework in the Green Card Sponsorship as a Retention Strategy post.


### DIY vs. Counsel — When a Startup Needs a Lawyer


The H-1B is not a form to file yourself. Denials, RFEs, and revocations are meaningfully higher for pro-se filings, and the downstream cost of a denial — a lost hire, a wasted lottery selection, a full year of delay — dwarfs the fee for competent counsel.


Fixed-fee immigration counsel at $2,500–$5,000 per H-1B petition is the right ballpark for a startup-focused firm. What good startup-focused counsel provides:


- Pre-filing eligibility screening (specialty occupation analysis, wage benchmarking, cap eligibility)
- LCA preparation and Public Access File setup
- Petition drafting with startup-specific evidence framing
- RFE response if USCIS requests more information
- Ongoing renewal, amendment, and worksite change support
- Support for concurrent green card sponsorship when it makes sense


Signs of a good fit for a startup:


- Fixed-fee pricing, not hourly billing
- Fast turnaround (48–72 hours to filing readiness once documents are complete)
- Comfort with early-stage documentation (fundraise announcements as evidence, small-company financials, founder-owned petitions)
- Ability to handle both employer sponsorship and founder self-petition tracks (H-1B and O-1A/EB-1A)
- A real case management portal, not just email chains


### The Bottom Line


A startup can sponsor an H-1B — at any stage, for founders, co-founders, or first hires. The 2025 H-1B Modernization Rule opened real pathways for founder-owned petitioners, and the standard H-1B remains a workhorse for hiring specialty-occupation candidates who don't yet qualify for O-1A.


The mistakes that trip up first-time sponsors are all preventable: ability-to-pay documentation, specialty-occupation framing, owner-beneficiary planning, real worksite documentation, PAF discipline, and calendar awareness for the March lottery. Get those six right and the H-1B is a straightforward operational function — not a legal risk.
